summary: Defines a RADIUS attribute that carries an IPv6 prefix to be delegated to the user. It can be used in either RADIUS or Diameter.

eli5.summary: When you sign in, the access server can hand you a block of IPv6 addresses for your home network. This is the RADIUS field used to say which block you get.

subtitle: A RADIUS attribute that tells an access server which IPv6 prefix to hand to a customer's own network.

tldr.problem: An existing RADIUS attribute for IPv6 prefixes was not designed to carry a prefix delegated for use inside the user's own network.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 4818 defines attribute type 123, Delegated-IPv6-Prefix, holding a prefix length from 0 to 128 bits and only as many prefix bytes as needed.
tldr.outcome: A delegating router can learn from the RADIUS server which prefix to pass on through DHCP Prefix Delegation. The attribute also works in Diameter.

today: RFC 4818 is a Proposed Standard, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why a New Attribute
sections.content:
RFC 4818 defines the Delegated-IPv6-Prefix attribute for RADIUS. It carries an IPv6 prefix that is to be delegated to the user, for use in the user's network. For example, the prefix can be handed to another node through DHCP Prefix Delegation (RFC 3633).

The existing Framed-IPv6-Prefix attribute is not designed to support delegation of prefixes for the user's network. For that reason, a RADIUS packet may contain both Framed-IPv6-Prefix and Delegated-IPv6-Prefix.
sections.eli5: There was already a label for the address block used on the connection itself. The home network needs its own block, so a second label was added.

sections.title: Attribute Format
sections.content:
The attribute has four header fields followed by the prefix. Type is 123. Length is the length of the whole attribute in bytes, at least 4 (a 0-bit prefix) and no larger than 20 (a 128-bit prefix). Reserved is always set to zero by the sender and ignored by the receiver. Prefix-Length is the length of the delegated prefix in bits, from 0 to 128.

The prefix field only needs to be long enough to hold the prefix bits, so it can be shorter than 16 bytes. Any bits in it that are not part of the prefix MUST be zero.
sections.eli5: The label says what kind of note it is, how long it is, and how much of the address block is yours. Short blocks use a shorter label.

sections.title: Where the Attribute Can Appear
sections.content:
In an Access-Accept packet the attribute MAY appear, and it can appear multiple times. In an Access-Request it MAY appear as a hint from the NAS that it would prefer those prefixes, but the server is not required to honor the hint. It MAY also appear in an Accounting-Request. It MUST NOT appear in any other RADIUS packet.

The RFC's example shows a requesting router sending a DHCP Solicit to the delegating router. The delegating router asks the RADIUS server, which answers with an Accept carrying the attribute. The delegating router then advertises the prefix and completes the DHCP exchange with a Reply.
sections.eli5: The access server can ask for a favorite block, but the company's computer makes the final decision and writes it in the approval note.

sections.title: Use in Diameter
sections.content:
In Diameter the attribute is an AVP from code space 1-255, the RADIUS attribute compatibility space, so no new Diameter code is allocated. Its data type is OctetString, and the AVP flag rules are M for MUST and P for MAY, with encryption set to Y.

The attribute needs no special translation between Diameter and RADIUS. It is copied as is, apart from changes to headers, alignment and padding. The RADIUS rules for Access-Request, Access-Accept and Accounting-Request apply to the matching Diameter messages.
sections.eli5: A newer system called Diameter can read the same label without any translation.

sections.title: Security and IANA Notes
sections.content:
The RFC adds no new security mechanism. It points to known RADIUS vulnerabilities discussed in RFC 2607, RFC 2865 and RFC 2869, and to RFC 3162 for using IPsec to protect RADIUS carried over IPv6. Diameter security is covered in RFC 3588.

On the IANA side, type value 123 was assigned from the RADIUS Attribute Types registry.
sections.eli5: This label does not add new locks. It relies on the protections that the existing system already has.

fields.name: Length
fields.desc: Whole attribute in bytes, from 4 to 20.

fields.name: Reserved
fields.desc: Zero from sender; ignored by receiver.
